250c779443.q: What is the origin story of a boutique commercial real estate advisory firm that specialized in Upper Manhattan and the Bronx before expanding citywide?
250c779443.a: Shimon Shkury started his career in 2002 at Massey Knuckle Realty and became a partner two years later. He met founding partners Victor Sozio, Ivan Petrovich, and Mike Tortorici at that firm. In the early 2000s, there was limited information about Upper Manhattan and the Bronx, so they focused on becoming the best information source for that territory. They felt they could expand this information advantage citywide and founded Ariel Property Advisors on January 10, 2011, right after the global financial crisis.
250c779443.e: 119. Celebrating 15 Years of Ariel Property Advisors in CRE with Shimon Shkury & Roxanne Donovan

06edf24e05.q: How does a commercial real estate advisory firm leverage information as a competitive advantage and why share market intelligence openly?
06edf24e05.a: Ariel Property Advisors uses an advisory-first approach, consolidating 15 years of information and 30 reports produced year over year into a centralized Salesforce database accessible to all 35 plus support and analysis staff. They share this information with competitors, reporters, and the market because they believe it benefits the greater good and the whole industry. They openly acknowledge that competitors cannot easily replicate their methodology, and artificial intelligence now helps them connect dots in their data in new ways to provide deeper analysis.
06edf24e05.e: 119. Celebrating 15 Years of Ariel Property Advisors in CRE with Shimon Shkury & Roxanne Donovan

a8b0680b61.q: What role do live events play in thought leadership and community engagement for a commercial real estate platform?
a8b0680b61.a: Coffee and Cap Rates is held twice a year in February and July, bringing together 30 market reports, quick market analysis, and industry players for discussion. The event has grown from 50 attendees to over 300 people, with 100% of proceeds plus matching funds going to Legal Outreach nonprofit, partnering with TD Bank. The event serves as a culmination of information and thought leadership while supporting nonprofit mission work and empowering clients and communities.
a8b0680b61.e: 119. Celebrating 15 Years of Ariel Property Advisors in CRE with Shimon Shkury & Roxanne Donovan

374f500b9b.q: How can a commercial real estate firm build company culture around social leadership and community involvement?
374f500b9b.a: Ariel Property Advisors calls this local leadership and discusses it every Monday morning, making nonprofit or professional organization involvement part of each team member's business plan. The founding partners model this by sitting on boards and attending events: Shkury serves on Israeli bonds and FIDF boards, Mike Tortorici works with Inner City for Catholic Kids, Victor Sozio sits on NYSAFA's board, and Sean Kelly organizes charity golf outings. All team members, junior and senior, participate and match their charitable giving, making it core to company culture.
374f500b9b.e: 119. Celebrating 15 Years of Ariel Property Advisors in CRE with Shimon Shkury & Roxanne Donovan

37c1d90162.q: What are the core values and operational practices that enable a real estate firm to rank among the best companies to work for nationally?
37c1d90162.a: Globe Street ranked Ariel as one of the best commercial real estate companies to work for, driven by their mission-based core values centered on one team, accountability, commitment, personal growth, and innovation. Shkury emphasizes working on culture daily by bringing teams together to resolve friction, creating a nurturing environment, and breaking silos by opening their Salesforce database so everyone sees everyone's work. They target two to five-year professionals who feel stalled elsewhere, offering 65 people supporting each individual's growth with internal encouragement rather than internal competition.

54ebc5388a.q: How should a commercial real estate advisory firm evaluate multi-year performance and respond during market downturns?
54ebc5388a.a: Rather than looking at single-year performance, Shkury advises examining the past three years: 2022 was good, but 2023 and 2024 were tough due to rising interest rates that stopped transactions. During downturns, the strategy is to talk to clients, advise them, hold their hand, and think through possibilities together. By 2025, when markets opened and Mayor Adams implemented City of Yes, 485X, and 467M for office conversions, Ariel was positioned to capture opportunities because relationships had been developed and maintained during the difficult period.

c113b68212.q: What market dynamics are driving Class A office demand and rent growth in major business districts?
c113b68212.a: Class A and Class A plus office transactions grew 25% year over year, with Class A average rent reaching about $85 per square foot and Class A plus above $100. A building on 57th Street is asking more than $300 per square foot for office penthouse space. There is significant demand and depth for premium office space with insufficient supply, which also drives competition in Class B office, making it harder to find available space than a year prior.

1bb8af520c.q: What regulatory and policy reforms are needed to address the affordable housing crisis in New York City?
1bb8af520c.a: Shkury argues that HSTPA needs reform or removal, requiring city and state to work together on whether to help landlords convert buildings to affordable housing, provide subsidies and tax breaks, create pathways to profitability for affordable housing, or provide private incentives for reinvestment. Without intervention, rent-stabilized buildings risk deterioration. Mayor Adams and Governor Hochul made progress with zoning changes, but more action is needed to increase housing supply and lower rents through production rather than regulation alone.
1bb8af520c.e: 119. Celebrating 15 Years of Ariel Property Advisors in CRE with Shimon Shkury & Roxanne Donovan

79b54d1788.q: Which international and domestic investor groups are currently seeking real estate opportunities in New York City?

97bf3d0023.q: How did policy alignment and tax incentives drive a 60% year-over-year increase in development transaction volume in Brooklyn during the first half of 2026?
97bf3d0023.a: The surge was driven by a combination of the 485 tax abatement program for projects under 99 units and the rezoning of the Atlantic Avenue corridor in Crown Heights and Bed-Stuy. Of the $1 billion in transactional volume, $300 million came from transactions in the greater downtown Brooklyn area, reflecting a flight to quality. Additionally, improved pricing across development sectors and increased land prices due to higher rents in supply-constrained markets contributed to the momentum.
97bf3d0023.e: 131. Brooklyn Real Estate: Development, Distress & Opportunity in 2026 featuring Sean R. Kelly, Esq.
f: Brooklyn's development sector surged with $1 billion in transaction volume during the first half of 2026—a 60% year-over-year jump —catalyzed by the 485 tax abatement program for projects under 99 units and the Atlantic Avenue corridor rezoning in Crown Heights and Bed-Stuy. Of that billion, $300 million came from the greater downtown Brooklyn area, signaling a deliberate flight to quality alongside improved pricing momentum across development sectors.
Policy alignment meets tax incentives: the formula for growth

The surge wasn't accidental. As Sean Kelly explains in the episode , two policy levers worked in concert: the 485 tax abatement program, designed specifically for smaller projects capped at 99 units, combined with the rezoning of the Atlantic Avenue corridor spanning Crown Heights and Bed-Stuyvesant. This pairing created a market-clearing environment where developers could model feasibility more reliably.

The 485 abatement is critical for projects under 100 units , because it removes the tax burden that would otherwise make smaller residential developments economically unworkable in Brooklyn's competitive land market. Zoning changes unlock land value; tax incentives unlock project feasibility.
Geography matters: the flight to quality reshapes Brooklyn development

Not all of Brooklyn's development growth distributed evenly. Of the $1 billion total, $300 million clustered in the greater downtown Brooklyn area —a concentration that reflects investor preference for established neighborhoods with stronger rental demand and tenant quality. Higher rents in supply-constrained neighborhoods drove land prices upward, accelerating the velocity of transactions.

50998060f6.q: What drove major office-to-residential conversion projects in Brooklyn's Navy Yard area post-COVID?
50998060f6.a: A large transaction in the Navy Yard in Clinton Hill, originally slated as an office conversion five to six years ago, was rezoned post-COVID when the office market struggled significantly. This rezoning allowed the owners to sell the site and likely exit whole while enabling the creation of approximately 700 units in a supply-constrained market with a strong job hub nearby.

The shift from office to housing in a post-pandemic landscape

What started five to six years ago as a straightforward office conversion project became something very different after 2020. As the pandemic reshaped commercial real estate fundamentals, the office market struggled significantly , leaving developers and property owners facing diminished prospects for traditional office conversions.

Rather than holding onto a project built for a market that no longer existed, the property owner pursued rezoning. This wasn't a standalone decision—it reflected a larger strategic pivot across Brooklyn's development landscape, where policy alignment with tax incentives created real opportunity in the multifamily sector. As explained in the full discussion on Coffee & Cap Rates , the combination of the 485 tax abatement program for projects under 99 units and broader rezoning initiatives in neighborhoods like Atlantic Avenue in Crown Heights created powerful incentives for this kind of conversion.

The Navy Yard project landed in a particularly favorable position: Clinton Hill sits near a strong job hub , and the supply of residential units in Brooklyn remained constrained relative to demand. Rezoning from office to residential transformed what could have been an abandoned asset into a meaningful contributor to housing supply.

9549225d00.q: What is driving long-term family owners and generational landlords to exit the rent-stabilized housing market in New York City?
9549225d00.a: Long-term owners, patient capital, and family offices—some of whom built buildings in Brooklyn generations ago—are exiting due to a combination of HSTPA regulations, increased operating costs, non-cooperating capital markets, and more recently, 0% rent increase orders. This is described as the first time in nearly 20 years of business that such an exodus of generational owners is occurring, representing a significant shift in the market.
9549225d00.e: 131. Brooklyn Real Estate: Development, Distress & Opportunity in 2026 featuring Sean R. Kelly, Esq.
f: Long-term family owners, patient capital, and family offices—some operating for generations in Brooklyn—are exiting the rent-stabilized market due to a confluence of HSTPA regulations, escalating operating costs, uncooperative capital markets, and most recently, 0% rent increase orders . This marks the first major exodus of generational owners in nearly 20 years, signaling a structural shift in the market's ownership composition.
The Perfect Storm: Regulations, Costs, and Frozen Rents

The exit of long-term owners reflects the cumulative weight of multiple pressures that have made rent-stabilized assets economically unviable. HSTPA (Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act) regulations have compressed owner flexibility , while operating costs—maintenance, labor, utilities—continue climbing without corresponding rental income growth. When paired with non-cooperating capital markets that refuse to finance rent-stabilized deals at acceptable returns, ownership becomes a burden rather than an asset.

The most recent blow came from zero-percent rent increase orders, which froze rental income entirely. For owners accustomed to modest annual increases that at least offset inflation, a complete freeze on revenue growth pushed many into liquidation mode. These weren't speculative investors—many built or acquired buildings decades ago in Brooklyn neighborhoods. Their patience capital had always absorbed market cycles, but this regulatory environment crossed a threshold.

As Sean Kelly explains in the episode , the sheer scale of this shift is unprecedented in his nearly two-decade career in Brooklyn real estate—a candid admission that this is not a cyclical correction, but a structural market change.

"We've experienced significant change in the rent stabilization housing stock since the passage of HSTPA, and this is the first time in my career—almost 20 years—that we're seeing long owners, patient capital, family offices exit."

dd1f4b4ed0.q: How do tax abatement programs like 467M incentivize office-to-residential conversions?
dd1f4b4ed0.a: The 467M tax abatement program allows developers to make economic sense of office-to-residential conversions while allowing the city to receive 25% of the…
dd1f4b4ed0.e: 127. NYC Investment Sales 1H 2026: Following the Capital, Not the Noise with Shimon Shkury
f: The 467M tax abatement program makes office-to-residential conversions economically viable for developers by offering substantial tax incentives, while simultaneously requiring 25% of the resulting units to be designated as affordable housing for the city. This dual benefit—developer profit and public housing gain—aligns the economics perfectly, creating significant transaction activity in the conversion space.

Tax abatement programs solve a fundamental problem: traditional office-to-residential conversions require developers to absorb substantial structural and systems costs with no guarantee of financial return. The 467M abatement removes that risk by reducing the tax burden on converted properties, making the arithmetic work for institutional and private investors alike. As Shimon Shkury explains in the episode , this policy design is deliberately creating alignment between developer incentives and municipal housing policy.

The affordability component is the lever that transforms tax policy into housing policy. By requiring one-quarter of units to remain affordable, New York City gains a steady stream of new affordable inventory without capital expenditure, while developers gain the tax relief they need to proceed. This structure has already generated approximately 16,000 units in the conversion pipeline over the past two years and fueled 65 office-to-residential transactions in that same period.

The scale of this activity reflects a broader shift in capital allocation. With the city facing a housing supply gap of roughly 60,000 units annually and only 30,000 being produced through conventional development, office conversions—particularly under incentive programs like 467M—have become a critical part of the supply solution. The podcast details how institutional investors view these deals as part of a reset valuation thesis, where older office stock can be repurposed into residential product with tax protection.
"Capital is investing in reset valuations, in fundamentals that are growing, in policy alignments. When all of those don't exist, capital is looking for distress and basis."

Interest rates and refinancing stress

Interest rates remain the top signal because they directly affect borrowing costs and investor returns. When rates rise, refinancing becomes painful for existing holders, opening the door to forced sales and distressed pricing. Mortgage maturity schedules tell you exactly when this pressure hits —watch which buildings have debt coming due at elevated rate environments, and whether owners can absorb higher payments or must exit.

Shimon Shkury explains in the episode that this dynamic is already reshaping valuations: free market multifamily buildings are trading at roughly 16% discounts to their peak valuations, even as rents have climbed 60% over six years. That gap exists precisely because financing costs have reset the math.
Economic signals and property fundamentals

Beyond rates, track broader economic health and stock market performance—these affect institutional investor appetite and capital availability. Fundamentals that grow independently of the macro cycle attract the most selective capital today. In multifamily, for example, rent growth decouples from economic cycles when demand outpaces supply.
